To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) institutional herding is intentional, 2) the degree of intentionality is higher for sectors with a high proportion of small capitalization firms, 3) herding is more pronounced during periods of high market volatility and 4) herding is higher during periods when the industry under examination underperformed.

institutional herding is intentional for most Spanish sectors and that herding intent is driven by the market state, with the exception of two sectors, namely the financial sector (which is driven by the sector state), and the utilities sector (which is not driven by any state variable).

institutional herding at an industry level is intentional for most industries, and that it is more likely to be intentional when the market as whole, or the specific industry under examination, has underperformed.

the herding phenomenon is more likely to be intentional than spurious in Spain, although it is more likely to occur during periods of poor market performance and high volatility.

institutional investors in the Spanish market tend to herd in order to avoid losses, and that this is particularly the case when the sector in question is experiencing poor performance.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the extent to which institutions herd at the sector level depends not only on the state of the market but also on the state of a specific sector, which is a novel contribution to the literature.
herding intent is sector-specific and not a general phenomenon.
herding at the sector level is not spurious, but intentional and driven by a combination of market and sector conditions.
